newsitem.title: USA: Natgas pipeline a boon to New England, study says.
newsitem.headline: Natgas pipeline a boon to New England, study says.

text.p: A proposed 640-mile natural gas pipeline running from Nova Scotia through Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts would create more than 3,330 jobs in the New England region by 1999, according to a study by its sponsors.

Construction of the pipeline, set to begin in 1997, would add $144 million to Maine personal income, increase property tax assessments, and result in the lower energy prices for the region, said the study by Cambridge, Mass.-based firm National Economic Research Associates, Inc.
A consortium of Mobil Oil Canada, Mobil Oil, Shell Canada, Nova Scotia Resources, Petro-Canada and Imperial Oil Ltd plans to start construction of the Maritimes & Northeast Pipeline next spring.

The pipeline would take natgas from an offshore field near Sable Island, Nova Scotia, and distribute it in Canada and northern New England. The consortium believes the natgas field is large enough to have production for a minimum of 25 years.
The line would have an initial capacity of 400 million cubic feet per day or enough gas to heat 1.2 million homes, said Jim Grasso, a spokesman for the consortium.

Andre Meade of National Economic Research Associates said in a telephone interview that fuel costs for "industrial users would certainly go down. But it's not 100 percent certain that rates for residential users will go down." As the region's utilities move toward deregulation, it is "unclear whether a reduction in fuel costs will result in a lower rate for consumers."

Meade's study concludes Maine would gain 3,330 jobs during the peak construction year of 1999. During that year, the project is estimated to add $157.19 million to the gross regional product and $144.37 million to Maine personal income taxes. Another 117 jobs would be added after construction was completed, according to the study.

Additionally, if construction begins as planned, New Hampshire would gain 469 jobs, $18.19 million in gross regional product and $16.72 million in personal income during 1997. After the construction is finished an additional 26 jobs would be created in the state.

And Massachusetts would gain some 179 jobs, $8.67 million to the gross regional product and $8.07 million in personal income during 1997. After construction, those figures drop to 66 jobs, $5.74 million of gross regional product and $5.53 million in personal income, according to the study.
